facts.F1: A scan reads 1 of 3 repos, pauses because the GitHub request budget is used up, and then resumes and reads the other 2. The queue then says "2 repos read", not 3. Each resume starts a new run that counts only its own reads. User decision (2026-11-21, option A): count the whole scan across its resumes (here "3 repos read"); the resumed run takes over the reads the paused run already saved.
facts.F10: The same whole-scan count is reported when the earlier run ended by interruption rather than by a used-up budget: after a resume of an interrupted scan, the queue reports the repos read by the interrupted run plus those read by the resuming run.

facts.F31: Priya is signed in with her GitHub account verified and has chosen three of her repos. facts.F34: Resume takes over the whole frozen plan. A resuming run records every non-skipped row of the paused run plan as its own plan, each row carrying the status it already holds, so the queue counts the reads of the whole scan and not only of the last run. The alternative, a scan-chain column counted across the runs of one scan, needs a stored schema change and a distinct-repo count to avoid counting a repo twice; the takeover needs neither.
facts.F35: One writer freezes the plan and its statuses. ScanRunPort record_plan takes plan rows with their status, so freezing the resuming run plan and carrying its already-read rows is one transaction. No second writer of scan_run_repos appears, and the mark-repo-read seam keeps its meaning: a read made now, by this run.
facts.F36: The count stays a set of plan positions. repos_read_of keeps counting the rows of the latest run whose status is read. A repo has one row per plan, so a repo read again by a resume after an unsaved read counts once, and no counter can be incremented twice.
facts.F37: The resume verdict owns each kept row status. The pure resume verdict in review-domain returns its kept rows as positions paired with the status the resuming run gives them: read for a row already read, planned for one it reads now or carries. The scan task maps those rows onto plan rows and writes them, and decides nothing about a row itself.
facts.F38: Carriers and their owners. ScanPlanRow carries one plan row and its status in ports; KeptRow carries one resume verdict row in review-domain; Resume carries the whole verdict; PlanRowStatus and ScanStatus carry row and run state; ReviewStoreError carries store refusals; the per-process scan state stays inside the scan task of the review app, under one admission per owner.
facts.F39: Each layer states what it owns. Domain: a frozen plan row is planned, read or skipped, and a resume maps the plan it resumes onto its own kept rows. Application: the scan task reads the planned rows in order, pauses on a low GitHub budget, and ends completed, rate limited or interrupted. Adapter: record_plan writes every kept row with its status in one transaction, mark_repo_read turns one row read, latest_scan counts the read rows of the latest run. Infrastructure: a refused or interrupted write leaves the rows the store already holds untouched and the run resumable.
facts.F4: A plan repo read again by a resume (because the earlier read was not saved) counts once, never twice.
facts.F40: Quint checks the count across resumes. The four count invariants are checked with quint verify over a three-row plan and twelve steps, because the claim is about state carried from run to run, not a proof over types: Agda would add nothing, and TLC is needed only for a temporal claim this design does not make.
facts.F41: A scan plan holds at most ten repos in total (SCAN_REPO_CAP, D-RRA-16), so a resume carries at most ten rows. The authority sets no lower bound: a plan of one row is admitted, and a plan of none is a run with nothing to count.
facts.F42: A plan row position and every stored count live in INTEGER columns: the adapter saturates a position or count above the signed 32-bit maximum and reads a negative one back as zero. This design keeps that existing bound and widens nothing.
facts.F43: Out of product scope: the words of the repos-read line, and a run kept from before scan plans were stored, which still says nothing about repos read.
facts.F44: Test budgets: each pure-core property case stays at or under 10 ms over at most 64 cases; the one acceptance scenario drives the real binary over HTTP and stays within a few seconds, the share ADR-091 already accepts for this family of review-app suites; the default cargo test suite keeps its 300 s ceiling.
facts.F45: The repos-read line is shown only for a completed run, so a paused or interrupted run shows no count at all. This design does not change that, and adds no count to an unfinished run.
